title: Every quadratic now has two roots

board_content.text: The discriminant is a weather forecast
Over $\mathbb{R}$, $x^{2}+1=0$ had no roots; over $\mathbb{C}$ it has two, $\pm i$.

board_content.caption: What the discriminant predicts (real coefficients)

board_content.text: $D>0$: two distinct real roots. $D=0$: one repeated real root.
$D<0$: two complex-conjugate roots — they have left the real line.
If $a,b,c$ are complex, the '$D<0$' classification is meaningless.

segments_english.text: This subtopic is where the whole chapter pays off. The quadratic formula that used to fail now always succeeds — the missing roots were complex all along.

Over the reals, x squared plus one equals zero had no solution. Over the complex numbers it has exactly two, plus i and minus i. This is the first glimpse of a deep fact: a degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots once you allow complex numbers.
The formula is the familiar one: x equals minus b plus or minus root D, all over two a, where D, the discriminant, is b squared minus four a c.
Think of D as a weather forecast. Before you solve anything, D tells you what kind of roots to expect, the way a monsoon forecast tells you whether to carry an umbrella.
If D is positive, you get two distinct real roots, both sitting on the number line. If D is zero, you get one repeated real root, right at minus b over two a.
And if D is negative, you get two complex-conjugate roots. The roots have left the real line and moved off into the plane, as a mirror-image pair.
One crucial caveat: this whole forecast table assumes the coefficients a, b, c are real numbers.
If the coefficients are themselves complex, the idea of D being negative doesn't even make sense, and the roots need not be conjugates. Keep that boundary firmly in mind.

segments_hinglish.text: Ye subtopic wahan hai jahan poora chapter pay off karta hai. Wo quadratic formula jo pehle fail hoti thi, ab hamesha succeed karti hai — missing roots hamesha se complex the.

Reals par, x squared plus one equals zero ka koi solution nahi tha. Complex numbers par iske theek do hain, plus i aur minus i. Ye ek deep fact ki pehli jhalak hai: degree-n polynomial ke theek n roots hote hain jab aap complex numbers allow karo.
Formula wahi familiar hai: x equals minus b plus or minus root D, poora over two a, jahan D, discriminant, hai b squared minus four a c.
D ko ek weather forecast samjho. Kuch bhi solve karne se pehle, D batata hai kis tarah ke roots expect karne hain, jaise monsoon forecast batata hai umbrella le jaana hai ya nahi.
Agar D positive hai, do distinct real roots milte hain, dono number line par. Agar D zero hai, ek repeated real root milta hai, theek minus b over two a par.
Aur agar D negative hai, do complex-conjugate roots milte hain. Roots real line chhodke plane mein chale gaye, ek mirror-image pair ki tarah.
Ek crucial caveat: ye poora forecast table maanta hai ki coefficients a, b, c real numbers hain.
Agar coefficients khud complex hain, to D ke negative hone ka idea sense hi nahi banata, aur roots conjugates hone zaroori nahi. Is boundary ko pakka dhyaan mein rakho.
